pedagogy.summary: This is the shared LANGUAGE of the fraction–decimal–percentage world: the terms decimal, decimal point, tenths/hundredths/thousandths, per cent and the % symbol, convert, terminating decimal — and, crucially, the understanding that a fraction, a decimal and a percentage are THREE NOTATIONS FOR ONE VALUE (1/2 = 0.5 = 50%). Fluency here is not reciting definitions but USING the words correctly in context: reading 0.09 as 'nine hundredths' (not 'point oh nine'), reading 50% as 'fifty out of a hundred', and moving between the three forms as names for the same amount. The place-value reading of decimals and the 'out of 100' meaning of per cent are the load-bearing habits; sloppy digit-string reading ('point oh nine') is where meaning leaks away.
bestPractices: Teach the three forms together as one value using a single quantity shown four ways — a shaded hundred square, the fraction (with denominator 100), the decimal, and a position on a 0%–100% number line — so 1/2, 0.5 and 50% are visibly the same.
Insist on place-value reading of decimals: 0.09 is 'nine hundredths', 0.7 is 'seven tenths', never 'point oh nine' or 'point seven', so the digits keep their meaning.
Model correct percentage language: per cent means 'out of / for every hundred'; 100% is the whole; write 'X% of N', never the bare 'X% = value'.
Use real contexts (sales '50% off', a half-full jug, test scores out of 100) and ask children to state the same fact as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
Introduce 'terminating decimal' and 'convert' as working vocabulary in the act of converting, so the words are attached to actions rather than defined in isolation.
keyRepresentations: Four-way display: shaded hundred square + fraction (n/100) + decimal + point on a 0%–100% number line
0–1 / 0%–100% double number line linking the three forms
Place-value chart for reading decimals aloud (ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths)
Real-context cards (50% off, jug 0.5 full, 3/4 of a pizza) matched across notations
Matching sets of fraction–decimal–percentage cards for one value
commonMisconceptions: Reading decimals as digit strings ('point oh nine', 'point seven') instead of place-value names ('nine hundredths', 'seven tenths').
Treating fraction, decimal and percentage as different, unrelated things rather than three names for one value.
Misusing percentage notation — writing '10% = 42' instead of '10% of 420 = 42'.
Reading the percentage number as the whole ('50% means 50') rather than as parts per hundred.
Confusing per cent (out of 100) with a plain count.

learn.summary: Teaches the shared language of fractions, decimals and percentages: that 1/2, 0.5 and 50% are three notations for ONE value, and that the words (tenths/hundredths/thousandths, per cent, % symbol, convert, terminating decimal) must be USED correctly in context, not just recited. The load-bearing habits are place-value reading of decimals (0.09 can be read 'nine hundredths'; the digit reading 'zero point zero nine' is also conventional, but the place-value name shows what it means) and the 'out of 100' meaning of per cent (writing '9% of £420 = £37.80', never '9% = £37.80', while equivalences such as '9% = 0.09' remain correct). The flagship activity ties one shaded quantity to its fraction, decimal, percentage and number-line position so all forms move together; alternatives (matching/diagnostic practice, explaining to a younger child, a labelled reference display) exercise and check the same vocabulary with different affordances.

activities.title: One quantity, three names — fill and watch them move together
feedback: If a learner reads 0.09 only as 'point oh nine', accept it as a valid digit reading, then point to the nine in the hundredths column and the 9/100 fraction and ask them to give the place-value name 'nine hundredths' too.
If a learner treats the forms as unrelated, highlight that one fill action moved all three labels and the number-line marker at once — one point, three names.
If a learner writes '9% = £37.80', recast as '9% OF £420 = £37.80' and show that 9% means 9 parts per hundred of the base £420, so 9% on its own is not £37.80.
activities.rationale: Manipulating a single quantity and watching the fraction, decimal, percentage and number-line marker update together couples the vocabulary to the relationship between representations, which is what using the terms in context requires. The live 'read it' voicing targets the digit-string misconception at the moment it would otherwise occur. This is a research-informed design proposal, not a tested intervention; a static or recorded display can also teach these links, though it cannot be re-driven from the learner's own action.
sourceClaims: Instruction should build the understanding that per cent means 'number of parts per hundred' and that percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents (three forms of one value); a documented notation error is writing 9% as 0.9 (remedied by reading 0.09 as 'nine hundredths' and 0.9 as 'nine tenths'), and pupils must write 'X% of N' rather than the bare 'X% = value'. Four parallel representations are recommended: the written percentage, a fraction with denominator 100, shading on a hundred square, and a position on a 0%–100% number line.
A percentage represents part of a quantity (an operator on a base), not a plain number; failing to keep this in view underlies base-neglect errors.
learnerActions: Fill a hundred square (or slide a bar) to show a chosen amount, e.g. drag to fill fifty squares.
Read the linked panel as it updates in lockstep: 50/100, 0.5, 50%, with a marker halfway along a 0%–100% number line.
Say the decimal aloud in place-value language ('five tenths, one half, fifty per cent'); use a 'read it' option to hear the correct reading.
Fill nine squares and confirm the panel reads 9/100, 0.09, 9% and voices the place-value name 'nine hundredths' alongside the digit reading 'zero point zero nine'.
Switch to context skins (a '9% off' price tag, a jug 0.5 full) and state the same fact as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
When finding part of an amount, practise saying and writing 'X% of N' (e.g. '9% of £420 = £37.80') rather than '9% = £37.80'; equivalences such as '9% = 0.09 = 9/100' are still correct.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction, a decimal and a percentage are not three separate topics but one quantity wearing three names; the correct place-value reading and the 'per cent = out of 100' meaning are visible in the same moment the learner acts.

activities.title: Match, read and complete — diagnostic usage practice
feedback: If 'nine tenths' or 'nine' is chosen for 0.09, state the place-value name 'nine hundredths' and point back to the hundredths place.
If equivalent forms are grouped wrongly, show the shared value on a hundred square or number line so the three cards name one point.
For '__% of 420 = 42', confirm 10% (since 1% of 420 = 4.20, so 10% of 420 = 42) and stress the phrase '10% OF 420'.
activities.rationale: Matching, reading-choice and fill-in tasks score correct usage and, with distractors drawn from the digit-string and base-neglect misconceptions, surface specific errors. They assess and rehearse usage rather than building the linked-representation habit, so they complement rather than replace the manipulable display.
sourceClaims: Instruction should build the understanding that per cent means 'number of parts per hundred' and that percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents (three forms of one value); a documented notation error is writing 9% as 0.9 (remedied by reading 0.09 as 'nine hundredths' and 0.9 as 'nine tenths'), and pupils must write 'X% of N' rather than the bare 'X% = value'. Four parallel representations are recommended: the written percentage, a fraction with denominator 100, shading on a hundred square, and a position on a 0%–100% number line.
A percentage represents part of a quantity (an operator on a base), not a plain number; failing to keep this in view underlies base-neglect errors.
learnerActions: Match cards so that each value's three forms are grouped, e.g. 1/2 ↔ 0.5 ↔ 50%.
Choose the correct place-value reading of a decimal, e.g. 'What is the place-value name for 0.09?' with 'nine tenths' or 'nine' offered as tempting wrong answers.
Complete 'X% of N' statements, e.g. fill the blank in '__% of 420 = 42'.
Sort a mixed set of cards by the single value each one names.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct use of the vocabulary is checkable: the right place-value reading, the right grouping of equivalent forms, and the correct 'X% of N' phrasing distinguish understanding from digit-string reading and base-neglect.

activities.title: Explain it to a younger child
feedback: If the learner says 'per cent means the number', prompt: 'out of how many?' to recover 'out of 100'.
If they claim 1/2 and 50% are different, ask them to shade half a hundred square and count the shaded squares as a percentage.
If they ignore the base when comparing 9% off and 50% off, ask '9% of what? 50% of what?' to surface that the amount depends on each item's price.
activities.rationale: Explaining a real sale or a half-full jug exercises genuine production of the vocabulary in context and can expose base-neglect. Spoken explanation does not display the forms updating together, so it supports practice alongside, not instead of, a representation that moves in lockstep.
sourceClaims: A percentage represents part of a quantity (an operator on a base), not a plain number; failing to keep this in view underlies base-neglect errors.
learnerActions: Explain a shop's '9% off' sign or a half-full jug to a younger character who asks 'what does per cent mean?' and 'is that the same as a half?'
Say a single quantity three ways (fraction, decimal, percentage) and read each aloud correctly.
Answer whether '9% off' could ever take off more money than '50% off', and say what it depends on (the base amount).
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed to explain forces the learner to produce and justify the three forms and the 'parts per hundred of a base' meaning in their own words.

activities.title: Four-way reference display
feedback: When a reading is unsure, tap to hear the place-value name and compare it with the shaded square.
Use the 'per cent = out of 100' flap whenever a learner starts treating the percentage number as the whole.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled display with tap-to-hear readings is a useful reference and models the four recommended representations. Because it shows one value at a time rather than being re-driven by the learner across many values, pair it with activities where the learner changes the quantity themselves.
sourceClaims: Instruction should build the understanding that per cent means 'number of parts per hundred' and that percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents (three forms of one value); a documented notation error is writing 9% as 0.9 (remedied by reading 0.09 as 'nine hundredths' and 0.9 as 'nine tenths'), and pupils must write 'X% of N' rather than the bare 'X% = value'. Four parallel representations are recommended: the written percentage, a fraction with denominator 100, shading on a hundred square, and a position on a 0%–100% number line.
learnerActions: Study one value shown four ways at once: shaded hundred square, fraction with denominator 100, decimal, and a point on a 0%–100% number line.
Tap each form to hear its correct reading (e.g. 'nine hundredths').
Open the flap on 'per cent = out of 100' to check the meaning.
activities.intendedInsight: Having the four parallel representations of one value side by side, each with its correct reading, gives a stable reference for the shared-value idea and place-value language.

constraints: Insist that learners can give the place-value reading of decimals: 0.09 is 'nine hundredths', 0.7 is 'seven tenths'. Digit readings such as 'zero point zero nine' or 'point seven' are conventional and not wrong, but they do not show place value, so always ask for the place-value name as well.

When finding a percentage of an amount, always write 'X% of N' (e.g. '9% of £420 = £37.80'), never '9% = £37.80', including in worked feedback; per cent means parts per hundred of a base, and 100% is the whole. Equivalences between forms, such as '9% = 0.09 = 9/100' or '50% = 0.5 = 1/2', are correct and should be encouraged.
Treat the three forms as names for one value, not as separate topics; show them together on a shaded hundred square and/or a 0%–100% number line.
Introduce 'terminating decimal' and 'convert' as working vocabulary during the act of converting, attached to actions rather than defined in isolation.
Matching, multiple-choice and sorting tasks check correct usage but do not by themselves build the linked-representation habit; use them alongside an activity where the learner drives the change.
A fixed reference display shows one value at a time and cannot be re-driven by the learner; pair it with manipulable work across many values.
The target is USE in context, not reciting definitions; judge success by how a learner reads, writes and moves between forms with real quantities.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (DfE National Curriculum, Years 4–6) carries verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed, and it was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims as a general statutory-requirement assertion rather than direct support for that activity's design principle.
Self-audit: 1% of 420 = 4.20, so 9% of 420 = 37.80 and 10% of 420 = 42; these figures from the source row are arithmetically consistent and were used as given.

The original row asserted '3D adds no meaning' and that 'dialogue cannot show the forms moving together' as near-absolute claims; these have been softened to affordance-based statements (a conversation produces spoken usage but no synchronised display), since catalog fit ratings do not establish comparative necessity or medium superiority.

The source's own example '9% off could be more than 50% off depending on the base' holds only across different base prices; the activity frames it explicitly as depending on the amount each percentage is taken of.
Fixed earlier: activity 2 feedback had modelled the forbidden bare notation '10% = 42'; it now reads '10% of 420 = 42', consistent with the 'X% of N' rule stated everywhere else.

probeDeeper: Read these aloud for me: 0.7, 0.07, 0.75. Now which fraction is each one?
If I say a bottle is 0.25 full and you say it's a quarter full, are we disagreeing? Why not?
Is it ever right to write '50% = 10'? When — and how should it be written properly?
The coat is '9% off'. Could 9% off ever be MORE money than 50% off? On what would that depend?
assess.correctAnswer: Half full = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, read as 'one half', 'five tenths / nought point five', 'fifty per cent'. 9% means nine out of every hundred (of the price); as a decimal 0.09; the money off is 9% OF £420, i.e. £37.80 (children may reason 1% of 420 = 4.20, so 9% = 37.80). The key usage: '9% of £420', never '9% = £37.80'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads decimals as digit strings — '0.09 is point oh nine', '0.5 is point five' — with no place-value meaning.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model place-value reading ('nine hundredths', 'five tenths') and tie each to the hundred square / place-value chart; have the child re-read in those terms. Reteach in place (no prerequisite gap named).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads decimals digit-by-digit; cannot say which fraction 0.09 or 0.5 is.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats fraction, decimal and percentage as different, unrelated things — does not accept 1/2, 0.5 and 50% as the same value.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show all three on one shaded hundred square / number line so they name one point; practise stating a single quantity three ways. Reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives one form but cannot supply the others for the same amount, or denies they are equal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misuses percentage notation — says '9% = £37.80' or '9% means 9', dropping the base.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on 'X% OF N' phrasing; per cent is parts per hundred OF a quantity; contrast '9%' with '9% of £420'. Reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes/says the percentage as a bare value without 'of the whole'; treats the % number as an absolute.

responseLevels.gap: Reads decimals as digit strings, treats the three forms as unrelated, and uses percentage as a bare number ('9% = 9'). Vocabulary is disconnected from meaning.
responseLevels.full: Reads decimals in place-value language, uses 'per cent'/'%' correctly as parts per hundred of a base ('9% of £420'), and treats fraction, decimal and percentage as three names for one value, converting between them in real contexts; transfers to unfamiliar quantities.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes each form and knows some equivalences (1/2 = 0.5 = 50%), but still reads a decimal as 'point five' rather than in place value, or cannot move fluently among all three forms in context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A jug is half full. Give me three different ways to say how full it is — as a fraction, as a decimal, and as a percentage — and read each one aloud the proper way. Then: a shop sign says '9% off a £420 coat'. Say what 9% means here, write it as a decimal, and tell me how much money comes off.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Listening for USE, not definitions: a child with the language reads 0.5 and 0.09 in place-value terms, treats 1/2, 0.5, 50% as one value, and says '9% OF £420'. A child without it reads 'point oh nine', treats the three forms as separate, or says '9% = 37.80' / '9% means 9'. The half-full context forces the three-forms-one-value link; the sale context forces correct per-cent-of-a-base usage.
